extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, philosophy, and literary theory interested in theories of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and critiquing competing theoretical criteria for when and why things are comic or provoke laughter (mechanical/expectation, release/liberty, Freud's wit/tendency wit), illustrated with examples and counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative disappointments as cause of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea (endorsed by some predecessors of Lipps and Spencer) that laughter arises from a discrepancy in quantity between expectation and reality — e.g., expecting a great thing and receiving a trivial one, with greater discrepancy producing stronger laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and limits provided: tiny departures should only provoke slight giggles, while extreme mismatches (too much or too little) can provoke uproarious laughter. The author argues this cannot be the sole explanation (it would predict continuous scaling of laughter with discrepancy) and gives counterexamples such as the juggler who alternately avoids then receives the apple blow, showing laughter can arise in both directions of expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychic weight / expectation-versus-arrival
rubrics_metrics.description: Lipps’s formulation that 'the comic resides in one's expecting for the aunt a worthy situation and finding an unworthy' — an account that invokes the notion of 'psychic weight' (some objects/events having greater psychic importance than others) to explain why certain incongruities are comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text critiques this by showing mechanical sequence matters (the man prepared psychic energy for a cat but found an aunt) and that 'psychic weight' is indeterminate; examples (cat vs aunt, cow in closet) illustrate difficulties. Use this criterion cautiously — it can explain some cases where a trivial arrival displaces a weightier expectation, but is vague and contestable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful annoyance / failure of adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter arises when an anticipated serious adjustment is prevented by a trivial or preposterous event, producing a playful annoyance that cannot be immediately reconciled — we laugh when the discrepancy robs us of the possibility of serious adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the clown who poises for a leap but merely saunters off, or the acrobat who repeatedly dodges apples and then finally receives a smash: small disappointments elicit little laughter; only when the mismatch becomes extreme enough to prevent normal cognitive/behavioral adjustment does comic laughter emerge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as liberty / release from constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory (Shaftesbury, Bain, Dewey, Renouvier, Penjon) that laughter is the result of a release of the nervous system from tension or constraint — a 'let-go' when a purpose or obstacle is suddenly removed. Humor signals a transition from the serious/rigid to the easy/free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers external (political/legal) and internal (mental, rational) constraints; Renouvier adds deliverance from constraints of rationality. Dewey frames laughter as 'a sudden relaxation of strain' marking attainment of unity. The author notes this release can 'flavor' humor but objects that many other actions follow release (stretching, sighing) and so release alone cannot uniquely define the comic; liberty may accelerate laughter but does not fully explain its specific tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: The uniqueness of the comic feeling (Lipps's 'feeling of the comic und weiter nichts')
rubrics_metrics.description: Lipps’s claim that 'The feeling of the comic is a feeling of the comic und weiter nichts' — i.e., the comic has a unique subjective tone that cannot be reduced to other affective states like mere relief or freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a diagnostic: the comic emotion has a distinctive quality that theories reducing laughter to other more general processes must account for. The author uses this claim to challenge purely negative/explanatory accounts (pure release or mere levity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freud: wit/jest/tendency-wit taxonomy (release of repressed tendencies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud’s classification: (a) play-like 'Scherz' or jest (nonsense that is pleasurable in itself), (b) 'wit' where nonsense acquires sense and value, and (c) 'tendency wit' where wit serves to release stronger repressed impulses (primarily the hostile/aggressive and sexual), thus producing laughter by gratifying forbidden tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jest: meaninglessness guarded from reason; Wit: nonsense that confers value to sense; Tendency wit: nonsense disguises expression of unconscious impulses so that they can be admitted socially. Use examples (Heine's 'famillionaire', 'Whose?' reply about taking a wife) to identify how obscene or hostile content is veiled. The author notes Freud sometimes overgeneralizes (reducing many forms to sex/aggression) and that this taxonomy explains why some jokes produce uproarious laughter (they release stronger impulses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Witticisms as disguise to permit forbidden content
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle that witty constructions (nonsense + sense) operate as disguises: the nonsense makes expression of socially or psychologically forbidden content tolerable, enabling gratification of suppressed impulses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when assessing humor that targets taboo subjects: if the form of the joke masks an aggressive or sexual implication, it can function as 'tendency wit' and produce stronger laughter by allowing the hearer to admit suppressed impulses under cover of playfulness. The author emphasizes this mechanism when explaining why some jokes provoke uproarious laughter while harmless jests do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit as dream-like condensation / economy of psychic expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud’s claim that wit resembles dreams (use of ambiguity, condensation, expressing multiple things by one form) and that wit produces pleasure by an 'unexpected economy of psychic expenditure' — a compression that conveys more meaning with less psychic work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud analyzes witticisms as instances of 'condensation' and 'economizing' techniques (punning, ambiguity, double meanings). The author is critical: sometimes the wit requires more psychic effort rather than less, and the 'economy' explanation is not always convincing. Use with caution; verify empirically whether decoding a witticism actually reduces psychic effort for the hearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Childhood word-play as foundation for adult wit
rubrics_metrics.description: The assertion that children's play with words and thoughts (sound-associations, rediscovery of the familiar, repetition) furnishes the original pleasure-source that adult wit formalizes and protects from censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing witty remarks, look for traces of childish play (repetition, sound-association, nonsense) that are reworked into socially acceptable forms; Freud and Groos are cited to support the developmental origin. This criterion links playful repetition and associative pleasure to later witty constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and counterexamples to single-factor theories
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's recurrent methodological criterion: no single mechanical or negative explanation (pure quantitative discrepancy, pure release/liberty, or pure economy-of-expenditure) suffices to account for the comic; theories must accommodate counterexamples (smiles of infants, laughter at deprivation of derision, laughter accompanied by admiration, various non-laughter reactions to release).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an evaluative test: subject any proposed theory to counterexamples drawn from the text (acrobat/apple example, aunt-in-closet, infant smile as assent). A robust account of humor should explain the unique tone of the comic and why some releases produce laughter while others produce different reactions (stretching, sighing, 'Whew!', etc.). The author repeatedly uses examples to disconfirm overgeneralized claims (e.g., Freud's economy claim, Penjon's liberty-as-all).
